evidenceAudit.scope: Women of reproductive age with a positive pregnancy test and pain or bleeding: recognising ectopic pregnancy, resuscitating rupture, and choosing expectant, medical (methotrexate) or surgical management. India has no dedicated national ectopic pregnancy guideline; clinical assessment and shock care follow the MoHFW safe abortion care (CAC) training and service delivery guidelines 2023, and thresholds and management criteria follow NICE NG126, with the methotrexate dose from the Oman Ministry of Health guideline (2021).

Symptoms, signs, transvaginal ultrasound findings, 48-hour hCG interpretation, criteria for expectant, methotrexate and surgical management, salpingectomy versus salpingotomy, follow-up and anti-D rules checked against NICE NG126 recommendations 1.3–1.7.

Single-dose methotrexate 50 mg/m² intramuscular, baseline tests, the day 4 to day 7 15% fall rule, second dose and post-treatment advice checked against the Oman Ministry of Health ectopic pregnancy guideline (2021), pp. 7–9.

pathophysiology.summary: An ectopic pregnancy implants outside the uterine cavity, usually in the fallopian tube. It cannot continue and can rupture, causing life-threatening intra-abdominal bleeding. Suspect it in any woman of reproductive age with a positive pregnancy test and abdominal pain, bleeding or collapse. Diagnosis combines transvaginal ultrasound with serial serum human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG). Stable women with small, unruptured ectopics can be managed expectantly or with methotrexate; rupture, pain, a fetal heartbeat or high hCG need surgery (NICE NG126).
keyMechanisms: Tubal damage (infection, surgery, previous ectopic) delays transport of the embryo, which implants in the tube.
The growing trophoblast erodes the thin tubal wall; rupture causes haemoperitoneum and shock.
Blood irritating the diaphragm causes shoulder-tip pain; pelvic blood causes rectal pressure.
Methotrexate stops trophoblast proliferation; success depends on low hCG and small mass size.

pathophysiology.summary: Miscarriage is loss of a pregnancy before viability; most early losses are due to chromosomal abnormalities. Retained products of conception cause continued bleeding and are the main route to infection. Post-abortion complications — haemorrhage, incomplete evacuation, uterine perforation and sepsis — remain an important cause of maternal death in India. Management depends on the woman's stability, the type of miscarriage and the presence of infection (CAC 2023).
keyMechanisms: Failure of the early pregnancy leads to separation of the gestational sac and bleeding from the placental bed.
Products left in the uterus stop it contracting, causing continued bleeding.
Retained tissue and breaks in asepsis allow ascending infection; sepsis can follow within 24–48 hours (NTG section 6.3).
Uterine instrumentation can cause perforation or cervical injury.

symptoms: Vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy, with or without passage of tissue

Fever with foul discharge and abdominal pain: septic abortion (NTG section 6.3)
Severe pain, rigidity or shoulder pain after a procedure: perforation (CAC 2023 p. 49)
Persistent pain unrelieved by analgesia: exclude ectopic pregnancy (CAC 2023 p. 60)
precipitants: Retained products after medical or surgical abortion

clinicalManagement.title: Stabilise
actions: Shock: open airway, oxygen 6–8 L/min, Ringer lactate 1 litre in 15–20 minutes through a 16–18 gauge cannula, keep warm, intravenous antibiotics, transfuse if needed (CAC 2023 p. 50).
Evacuate retained products if suspected once resuscitation starts (CAC 2023 p. 50).

clinicalManagement.title: Control bleeding
actions: Misoprostol and uterine massage for uterine bleeding (CAC 2023 p. 49).
Continuing bleeding: oxytocin 10 units in 500 mL Ringer lactate or normal saline at 40–60 drops/min (CAC 2023 p. 49).
Cervical tear: pressure, then absorbable suture (CAC 2023 p. 49).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat retained products
actions: Incomplete abortion: misoprostol or vacuum aspiration up to 12 weeks under antibiotic cover (CAC 2023 pp. 38, 51).
Missed miscarriage: expectant for 7–14 days, or mifepristone then misoprostol, or vacuum aspiration (NICE 1.5.4, 1.5.11).

clinicalManagement.title: Septic abortion
actions: Blood and cervical cultures, then intravenous antibiotics (NTG section 6.3).
Evacuate retained products; it is crucial for response (NTG section 6.3). Take care: an infected uterus perforates more easily (CAC 2023 p. 51).

clinicalManagement.title: Before discharge
actions: Anti-D for Rh-negative women; iron-folic acid for 3 months; contraception counselling (CAC 2023 p. 47).
Follow-up in 1–2 weeks (CAC 2023 p. 47).

pathophysiology.summary: Maternal sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by infection during pregnancy, childbirth, after abortion or in the postpartum period. Common sources are the genital tract (endometritis, chorioamnionitis, septic abortion), urinary tract, lungs, breast and wounds. Normal pregnancy changes mask early signs, so deterioration can be sudden. Treat as an emergency: antibiotics within an hour, fluids, vasopressors if needed, and early source control (SMFM 2023; NTG 2025).
keyMechanisms: Organisms ascend from the vagina into the uterus after delivery, procedures or retained tissue.
A dysregulated host response causes vasodilatation, capillary leak and organ hypoperfusion; lactate rises.
Pregnancy lowers colloid oncotic pressure, so aggressive fluids cause pulmonary oedema more easily (SMFM p. B10).
Group A streptococcus and clostridia can cause rapid toxic shock and necrotising infection (NTG section 6.8).

symptoms: Fever or chills; feeling very unwell
Pelvic pain (NTG section 6.8)
Foul-smelling or purulent vaginal discharge (NTG section 6.8)
Breathlessness, confusion, reduced urine output
physicalSigns: Oral temperature 38.5°C or higher (NTG section 6.8)

redFlags: Mean arterial pressure under 65 mmHg or lactate over 2 mmol/L after fluids: septic shock (SMFM p. B3)

Rapid spreading skin changes or severe pain out of proportion: necrotising infection (SMFM Table 4)
Fetal tachycardia or distress in antenatal sepsis
precipitants: Prolonged rupture of membranes and prolonged labour
Caesarean birth, retained placenta or products

clinicalManagement.title: First-hour bundle
actions: Cultures and lactate, then broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics (SMFM rec 8; Figure 2).
Start 1–2 L balanced crystalloid over the first 3 hours; reassess often (SMFM rec 10–11).
Treat as an emergency: senior obstetric, anaesthetic and critical care review (SMFM rec 2).

clinicalManagement.title: Septic shock
actions: Norepinephrine to keep mean arterial pressure at 65 mmHg if hypotension persists (SMFM rec 14; Figure 2).
Hydrocortisone if no response to norepinephrine or epinephrine 0.25 micrograms/kg/min or more for at least 4 hours (SMFM Figure 2).
Transfer to intensive care unit (ICU) or high-dependency care.

clinicalManagement.title: Source control
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as a source is found
actions: Evacuate retained products, drain abscesses, deliver if intra-amniotic infection, regardless of gestational age when the uterus is the source (SMFM rec 9, 18).
Necrotising infection or myometrial necrosis: debridement and hysterectomy (SMFM p. B9).

clinicalManagement.title: Ongoing care
actions: De-escalate antibiotics with culture results; daily review (SMFM p. B9).
Pharmacological thromboprophylaxis in septic shock (SMFM rec 16); insulin if glucose over 180 mg/dL (SMFM rec 17); early enteral feeding (SMFM Figure 2).
Breastfeeding usually continues; check drug compatibility.

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults and children in India with hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) persisting for 6 months or more: assessment, who to treat under the National Viral Hepatitis Control Program (NVHCP), choice and dosing of tenofovir or entecavir, monitoring, pregnancy and prevention of mother-to-child transmission, and co-infection with HIV or hepatitis C. Built on the NVHCP Technical Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Hepatitis B (2019).

Adult and paediatric doses of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), entecavir and tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) and rules for choosing between them checked against Tables 2 and 3, p. 23.
Baseline and follow-up tests, referral to Model Treatment Centres, pregnancy, birth-dose vaccine and hepatitis B immunoglobulin, breastfeeding and children checked against pp. 24–25.
HIV co-infection (tenofovir-based antiretroviral therapy), hepatitis C co-infection and prevention checked against pp. 26–27; renal monitoring and entecavir renal dosing against p. 47.
Not clinically reviewed.
unverifiedSections: TDF dose interval in reduced creatinine clearance is not given in the NVHCP guideline; the guideline advises entecavir or TAF when eGFR is under 60 mL/min/1.73 m².
Antiviral prophylaxis in pregnancy for high viral load is described as unclear in NVHCP 2019; follow current specialist advice.
Hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance interval is not stated explicitly in the NVHCP sections used; ultrasound is part of baseline assessment.

The fixed-dose antiretroviral tablet strengths (TDF 300 mg, lamivudine 300 mg, efavirenz 600 mg) are not stated in NVHCP 2019; the National AIDS Control Organisation now favours dolutegravir-based tenofovir regimens — follow the current national ART guideline.
Pegylated interferon is for selected patients at Model Treatment Centres; dosing is not given here.

pathophysiology.summary: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) is defined by HBsAg persisting for 6 months or more. India has intermediate endemicity; most infections are acquired at birth or in early childhood, when about 90% of infected newborns become chronic carriers. Many people stay well for years, but some develop cirrhosis, liver failure or hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Antivirals suppress the virus and prevent progression but rarely cure, so treatment is usually lifelong (NVHCP 2019, p. 18).
keyMechanisms: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) persists in hepatocytes as covalently closed circular DNA, which drugs do not eradicate.
Immune attack on infected hepatocytes causes inflammation (raised ALT) and progressive fibrosis.
Fibrosis leads to cirrhosis, portal hypertension and decompensation.
Integrated viral DNA and chronic inflammation drive HCC, even without cirrhosis.

symptoms: Usually none; found on screening (antenatal, blood donation, pre-surgery) (NVHCP p. 18)
Fatigue, right upper abdominal discomfort
Jaundice, abdominal swelling or confusion in advanced disease
physicalSigns: Often normal examination
Signs of chronic liver disease: palmar erythema, spider naevi
Ascites, pedal oedema in decompensation (NVHCP p. 26)
redFlags: Jaundice, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy or variceal bleeding: decompensated cirrhosis — refer to Model Treatment Centre (NVHCP p. 24)
Flare with jaundice or acute liver failure (NVHCP p. 24)
Stopping tenofovir in HIV co-infection: risk of severe flare (NVHCP p. 27)
Starting chemotherapy or immunosuppression: reactivation risk (NVHCP p. 24)
precipitants: Perinatal transmission from an infected mother (NVHCP p. 18)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Recent exposure within 180 days and high ALT; repeat HBsAg after 6 months to confirm chronicity (NVHCP p. 22).
Anti-HCV positive with detectable HCV RNA.
HBsAg negative; fatty liver on ultrasound with metabolic risk factors.
Alcohol history; AST:ALT ratio often over 2.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: HBsAg positive for 6 months or more.
APRI 2 or more, or FIB-4 3.25 or more, or elastography 12.5 kPa or more.
APRI over 1.5, or FIB-4 over 1.45, or elastography 8.0 kPa or more.

Cirrhosis: treat irrespective of age, ALT, HBeAg or HBV DNA. Non-cirrhotic: treat if HBV DNA over 20,000 IU/mL with persistently raised ALT, or HBV DNA over 2,000 IU/mL with APRI over 1.5, FIB-4 over 1.45 or platelets under 100 ×10⁹/L, particularly if over 30 years.
At least 2 values 4 weeks apart in the last 6 months above the upper limit of normal.

pathophysiology.summary: Hepatitis C is a blood-borne RNA virus. Most people infected develop chronic infection without symptoms, and over years some progress to cirrhosis, liver failure and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), at 2–4% per year once cirrhotic (NVHCP p. 34). Oral direct-acting antivirals achieve sustained virological response in over 95% (NVHCP p. 41), and every person with detectable HCV RNA should be treated (NVHCP p. 36).
keyMechanisms: HCV replicates in hepatocytes; chronic immune-mediated injury causes inflammation and fibrosis.
Fibrosis progresses faster with alcohol, male sex, HIV or HBV co-infection and immunosuppression (NVHCP p. 35).
Extrahepatic effects include cryoglobulinaemia, glomerulonephritis, insulin resistance and lichen planus (NVHCP p. 35).
DAAs block viral NS5A and NS5B proteins; SVR12 equals cure.

symptoms: Usually none; found on screening (NVHCP p. 34)
Fatigue, cognitive problems, depression (NVHCP p. 35)
Jaundice, abdominal swelling, confusion or bleeding in decompensated cirrhosis
physicalSigns: Often normal
Stigmata of chronic liver disease
Ascites, jaundice, encephalopathy (decompensation) (NVHCP p. 39)
Purpura or rash from cryoglobulinaemia (NVHCP p. 35)
redFlags: Ascites, jaundice, encephalopathy or variceal bleeding (Child-Pugh B or C): refer to a Model Treatment Centre (NVHCP p. 39)
Taking amiodarone: sofosbuvir is contraindicated (bradycardia) (NVHCP p. 38)
HBV co-infection: risk of HBV reactivation during HCV treatment
Liver mass on ultrasound: suspected HCC
precipitants: Injecting drug use with shared equipment (NVHCP p. 34)
Blood transfusion before routine screening; frequent transfusion (thalassaemia, dialysis) (NVHCP p. 34)
HIV infection; men who have sex with men; sex work (NVHCP p. 34)

title: Rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease (India)

evidenceAudit.scope: Children and adults in India with acute rheumatic fever (ARF) or established rheumatic heart disease (RHD): diagnosis with the revised Jones criteria for moderate- and high-risk populations, eradication of group A streptococcus, anti-inflammatory treatment by manifestation, and secondary prophylaxis with its duration. Built on the ICMR Standard Treatment Workflow for Acute Rheumatic Fever (July 2024) and the NCDC-ICMR National Treatment Guidelines (2025) section 1.4.
findings: Pathophysiology, major manifestations with frequencies, Jones criteria for low-risk and moderate/high-risk populations, laboratory investigations and differentials checked against ICMR ARF STW (July 2024), page 1.

Primary prophylaxis (benzathine penicillin G by weight, penicillin V, amoxicillin, erythromycin), anti-inflammatory schedule (prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day for moderate/severe carditis; aspirin 75–100 mg/kg/day or naproxen 10–20 mg/kg/day), chorea treatment and secondary prophylaxis drugs and duration checked against the STW page 2.
Benzathine penicillin G every 3 weeks for secondary prophylaxis, and azithromycin for confirmed penicillin allergy, checked against NCDC-ICMR NTG 2025 section 1.4.
The STW and NTG differ on penicillin V dosing and allergy alternatives; shown side by side.
Not clinically reviewed.
unverifiedSections: The STW does not state the interval for benzathine penicillin G secondary prophylaxis; the 3-weekly interval is from NCDC-ICMR NTG.
Heart failure drugs (diuretics, digoxin, vasodilators) are named in the STW without doses; dose them per the heart failure topic and paediatric cardiology advice.
Anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation or mechanical valves, infective endocarditis prevention, and timing of valve intervention in established RHD are not covered in the sources used.
Penicillin V weight bands (27 kg or less: 250 mg; over 27 kg: 500 mg) were read from the STW poster image and match its benzathine penicillin bands; confirm against the original before use.
Adult anti-inflammatory doses are not separately stated; the weight-based doses apply to children and adolescents.
Drug cautions and contraindications without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.
US labels (DailyMed) were used where Indian sources give no dose; confirm against the Indian product label (CDSCO) and hospital formulary.

pathophysiology.summary: Acute rheumatic fever is an immune reaction that follows untreated or partly treated group A streptococcal (GAS) throat infection, mainly in children aged 5–15 years. It inflames the joints, heart, brain and skin. Repeated attacks scar the heart valves, causing rheumatic heart disease, still a major cause of heart failure, stroke and maternal death in India. Regular benzathine penicillin prevents recurrences and progression (ICMR ARF STW 2024).
keyMechanisms: Molecular mimicry between streptococcal antigens and heart, joint and brain tissue, plus an exaggerated T-cell response (ICMR STW).
Overcrowding, poor hygiene and limited access to care allow repeated GAS infections (ICMR STW).
Each recurrence adds valve damage; mitral regurgitation and stenosis are typical.
Valve disease leads to heart failure, atrial fibrillation and embolic stroke.

symptoms: Migratory pain and swelling of large joints (ankles, knees, wrists), each lasting under a week (ICMR STW)
Breathlessness, palpitations, fatigue (carditis or heart failure) (ICMR STW)
Involuntary jerky movements, clumsy handwriting, emotional lability 2–6 months after sore throat (chorea) (ICMR STW)
Fever after a recent sore throat
physicalSigns: Tender, red, swollen joints that respond quickly to NSAIDs (ICMR STW)
Tachycardia, new murmur, signs of heart failure (ICMR STW)
Erythema marginatum: pink rings with pale centres on trunk and limbs (ICMR STW)
Painless pea-sized subcutaneous nodules over extensor surfaces (ICMR STW)
redFlags: Heart failure or moderate/severe carditis (ICMR STW)
No response to treatment: refer to an ARF/RHD expert (ICMR STW)
Missed benzathine penicillin doses in known RHD
Pregnancy in a woman with RHD
precipitants: Untreated or partly treated streptococcal sore throat (ICMR STW)
Poor access to health care (ICMR STW)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Small joints, poor response to NSAIDs (ICMR STW).
Persistent, non-migratory arthritis (ICMR STW).
Fever with murmur, positive blood cultures (ICMR STW).

differentials.condition: Paediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorder with streptococcal infection (PANDAS)
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Tics or obsessive-compulsive symptoms rather than chorea (ICMR STW).

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Major criteria, moderate/high-risk populations such as India (ICMR STW)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Carditis (clinical and/or subclinical on echocardiography), arthritis (monoarthritis, polyarthritis or polyarthralgia), chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules.
Monoarthralgia; fever 38°C or more; ESR over 30 mm/h and/or CRP 3 mg/dL or more; prolonged PR interval for age (unless carditis is a major criterion).
Evidence of preceding GAS infection: positive throat culture or antigen test, or raised ASO titre (over 320 U).
Initial ARF: 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor. Recurrent ARF: 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor, or 3 minor.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Mitral or aortic regurgitation, valve thickening, stenosis
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Detects clinical and subclinical carditis, a major criterion (ICMR STW).

title: Breast cancer screening and breast-lump referral (India)

evidenceAudit.scope: Women in India aged 30–65 years in population-based screening, and any woman or man with a breast symptom: clinical breast examination (CBE), what counts as a positive screen, triple assessment, referral by level of care, and the treatment pathway after diagnosis, including adjuvant endocrine therapy that primary care may continue. Built on the MoHFW Operational Framework for Management of Common Cancers (2016) and the ICMR Standard Treatment Workflow for Breast Cancer (July 2020); endocrine drug doses from US labels where ICMR gives none.
findings: Screening women aged 30–65 years by CBE once every 5 years at sub-centres and Health and Wellness Centres by trained ANMs, referral of a palpable lump or nipple discharge to a surgeon at the CHC or district hospital, ultrasound confirmation, mammography from 35 years where available, and core biopsy preferred over fine needle aspiration cytology checked against the MoHFW Operational Framework 2016 (Table 1 p. 7; Section 1 pp. 6–10; Annexure 1a p. 15).

Symptoms and signs, red flags (do not ignore breast change; no excision biopsy for diagnosis; no biopsy before imaging), triple assessment, receptor testing, staging, treatment by stage and endocrine therapy for hormone receptor-positive disease checked against the ICMR Breast Cancer STW (July 2020).
Tamoxifen 20 mg/day for 5 years, letrozole 2.5 mg daily and anastrozole 1 mg daily with their renal, hepatic and monitoring statements checked against US prescribing information (DailyMed).
The framework and the STW differ on the age to add mammography; shown side by side.
Not clinically reviewed.
unverifiedSections: The ICMR STW does not say whether tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor is preferred after menopause; tamoxifen is marked preferred because it is listed first.
Chemotherapy, trastuzumab and bone-modifying agent doses are not given in the STW and are oncology-initiated; they are not listed as medicine rows.
Breast cancer risk factors and male breast cancer are not detailed in the framework sections used.
Ultrasound age thresholds and BI-RADS categories are not stated in the ICMR STW.
Mastitis and breast abscess management is not covered by the sources used.
Drug cautions and contraindications without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.
US labels (DailyMed) were used where Indian sources give no dose; confirm against the Indian product label (CDSCO) and hospital formulary.

pathophysiology.summary: Breast cancer often presents late in India. The's national programme screens women aged 30–65 years with clinical breast examination every 5 years, because mammography is not available at scale. Any lump, nipple change or skin change needs triple assessment: clinical examination, imaging (ultrasound with or without mammography) and core needle biopsy. Early detection allows breast-conserving surgery and curative treatment (MoHFW 2016; ICMR STW 2020).
keyMechanisms: Malignant epithelial cells proliferate in the ducts or lobules and invade surrounding tissue, forming a hard, irregular lump.
Invasion of skin and suspensory ligaments causes dimpling, peau d'orange, nipple retraction and ulceration (ICMR STW).
Lymphatic spread involves axillary then supraclavicular nodes (ICMR STW).
Hormone receptor-positive tumours depend on oestrogen, which is why tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors work.

symptoms: Breast lump, often painless (ICMR STW)
Nipple discharge, especially bloody (MoHFW Annexure 1a)
Change in breast shape or skin (ICMR STW)

physicalSigns: Hard irregular lump; asymmetry (ICMR STW)
Skin dimpling, oedema, ulcer, satellite nodules; nipple retraction (ICMR STW)

redFlags: Any breast or nipple-areola change: do not ignore (ICMR STW)
Skin ulceration, chest wall fixation, fixed axillary nodes (ICMR STW)
Supraclavicular nodes (ICMR STW)
Bone pain, jaundice or breathlessness in a woman with breast cancer (ICMR STW)
precipitants: Increasing age (screening yield higher over 40) (MoHFW Section 1)
